key_insight: Raising argon flow from 1600 to 1800 L/h during air plasma spraying produced thicker, denser NiCrFeBSiC coatings with better wear performance.
engineering_relevance: Argon flow is a practical process lever for improving coating build quality, hardness-related performance, and tribological resistance in thermal spray applications.
method: Air plasma sprayed self-fluxing NiCrFeBSiC metal-ceramic coatings at two argon flow rates: 1600 and 1800 L/h.
Characterized structure and properties using microhardness, elastic modulus, porosity/thickness assessment, ball-on-disk tribology, and scratch adhesion testing.
Compared coating failure behavior and wear response across both spray regimes.
evidence_signal: The 1800 L/h condition roughly doubled coating thickness, halved porosity, and reduced the friction coefficient to about 0.107, while scratch tests indicated strong adhesion with similar critical loads for both cases.
watch_item: The study compares only two argon flow settings, so the reported improvement may not capture the full process window or long-term service behavior.
paper_title: EFFECT OF ARGON FLOW RATE DURING AIR PLASMA SPRAYING ON THE STRUCTURE AND PROPERTIES OF NICRFEBSIC COATINGS
